subject: math
title: Probability: Fractions, the Probability Line, Experiments and Fair Games
seo_title: Grade 5 Probability Worksheets: Fractions, Probability Line and Experiments (Free, Answer Key)
standard_text: Use fractions to express the probability of events happening, represent this probability on a probability line, and use it to make predictions and informed decisions
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 math worksheets on probability for the Ontario curriculum: probability as a fraction, the probability line from 0 to 1, spinners, number cubes and bags, theoretical vs experimental probability, predictions and fair games. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Probability = the outcomes you want ÷ all the outcomes. It is a fraction from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
key_sub: 3 red and 5 blue marbles: P(red) = 3/8, not 3/5. On a spinner, look at the size of each part, not the number of colours. More trials get closer to the theory.
body_html:
Probability as a fraction

Probability tells how likely something is to happen. When the outcomes are equally likely:

probability = number of outcomes you want ÷ total number of outcomes

Example 1

What is the probability of taking a red marble from this bag?

There are 3 red marbles and 8 marbles altogether. Compare with all 8, not with the 5 blue.

Answer: 38

The probability line

A probability is a number from 0 to 1. 0 means impossible. 1 means certain. Halfway, 12, means equally likely to happen or not. A probability is never more than 1.

Example 2

You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. Where does rolling a number greater than 4 go on the line?

5 and 6 are greater than 4: 2 of the 6 outcomes. 26 is less than 36 = 12.

Answer: 26, between 0 and 12: unlikely

Spinners: look at the size of the parts

Example 3

What is the probability of landing on red?

Red covers half of the spinner. Do not count colours: 3 colours does not mean 13 each.

Answer: 12

Theoretical and experimental probability

The theoretical probability is what should happen, found by counting outcomes. The experimental probability is what did happen: number of times it happened ÷ number of trials. They are usually close, but rarely exactly the same. More trials usually get closer.

Coin tossesHeadsExperimental probability
107710
209920
200104104200
Example 4

You roll a number cube 60 times. About how many 6s should you expect?

A 6 has a probability of 16. 16 of 60 is 60 ÷ 6 = 10.

Answer: about 10

Fair games

A game is fair when every player has the same probability of winning. Win on even, lose on odd with a number cube: 36 and 36, so it is fair.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
3 red, 5 blue, so P(red) = 35.Compare with ALL the outcomes: 38.
3 colours, so each colour is 13.Look at the size of each part of the spinner.
“Less than 3” on a number cube is 1, 2 and 3.List the outcomes carefully: only 1 and 2.
“5 tails in a row, so heads is due.”A coin has no memory. Heads is still 12.

faq.q: What do Grade 5 students learn about probability in the Ontario math curriculum?
faq.a: In Grade 5 (Data, D2), students use fractions to describe the probability of an event, place it on a probability line from 0 to 1, and use it to make predictions and decisions. They also find and compare the theoretical and experimental probability of an event.

faq.q: How do you write a probability as a fraction?
faq.a: Put the number of outcomes you want over the total number of outcomes. A bag with 3 red and 5 blue marbles gives a probability of 3/8 for red, not 3/5.
A probability line is a number line from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), with 1/2 meaning equally likely. Students place a probability such as 3/4 on it to show how likely an event is.

faq.q: What is the difference between theoretical and experimental probability?
faq.a: Theoretical probability is what should happen, found by counting outcomes. Experimental probability is what actually happened in trials, such as 9 heads in 20 tosses (9/20). With more trials, the two usually get closer.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a 3?
items.e: There are 6 equally likely outcomes and only one of them is 3: 16. 36 uses the number 3 as the count, but only one face shows a 3. 61 is upside down.

items.q: The spinner has 5 equal sections. What is the probability of landing on 4?
items.e: 4 is on 1 of the 5 equal sections: 15. 14 compares the 4 with the other 4 sections, not with all 5.

items.q: Cards numbered 1 to 10 are shuffled. You pick one without looking. What is the probability of picking the 7?
items.e: There is one 7 card out of 10 cards: 110. 710 would be the chance of picking a number from 1 to 7.

items.q: A bag has 2 red and 3 blue marbles. You take one without looking. What is the probability of red?
items.e: There are 2 + 3 = 5 marbles and 2 are red: 25. 23 compares red with blue, not with all 5 marbles. Two colours does not mean 12.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling an even number?
items.e: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6: 3 of the 6 outcomes, so 36. 26 forgets that 6 is even too. 63 is upside down.

items.q: The spinner has 6 equal sections: R is red and B is blue. What is the probability of red?
items.e: 2 of the 6 equal sections are red: 26. 24 compares red with blue. 46 is blue. 62 is upside down.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a number less than 3?
items.e: Less than 3 means 1 or 2: 2 of the 6 outcomes, so 26. 36 wrongly counts the 3. 46 is the chance of 3 or more.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of NOT rolling a 6?
items.e: Not a 6 means 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5: 5 of the 6 outcomes, so 56. 16 is the chance of rolling a 6.

items.q: Cards numbered 1 to 10 are shuffled. You pick one. What is the probability of an even number?
items.e: The even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10: 5 of the 10 cards, so 510. 410 forgets the 10. 55 compares even cards with odd cards.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. Which outcome has a probability of 36?
items.e: The odd numbers are 1, 3 and 5: 3 of the 6 outcomes. So rolling an odd number has a probability of 36. Rolling a 3 is only 16.

items.q: The spinner has 8 equal sections. What is the probability of landing on an odd number?
items.e: The odd numbers are 1, 3, 5 and 7: 4 of the 8 sections, so 48. 38 forgets the 1. 44 compares odd with even.

items.q: Cards numbered 1 to 8 are shuffled. You pick one. What is the probability of a number greater than 5?
items.e: Greater than 5 means 6, 7 or 8: 3 of the 8 cards, so 38. 48 wrongly counts the 5. 58 is the chance of 5 or less.

items.q: You take one marble without looking. What is the probability of green?
items.e: There are 4 + 1 + 3 = 8 marbles and 4 are green: 48. 44 compares green with the other 4 marbles. 13 counts colours, not marbles.

items.q: A bag has 3 red, 5 blue and 2 yellow marbles. What is the probability of NOT taking red?
items.e: Not red means blue or yellow: 5 + 2 = 7 of the 10 marbles, so 710. 510 forgets the yellow marbles. 310 is the chance of red.

items.q: The letters of CANADA are written on 6 cards. You pick one card without looking. What is the probability of A?
items.e: CANADA has 6 letters and 3 of them are A: 36. 14 counts the 4 different letters, but A is on 3 cards. 33 compares the A cards with the other 3 cards.

items.q: The letters of OTTAWA are written on 6 cards. You pick one card without looking. What is the probability of T?
items.e: OTTAWA has 6 letters and 2 of them are T: 26. 14 counts the 4 different letters (O, T, A, W). 24 compares the T cards with the other 4 cards.

items.q: Cards numbered 1 to 12 are shuffled. You pick one. What is the probability of a multiple of 4?
items.e: The multiples of 4 are 4, 8 and 12: 3 of the 12 cards, so 312. 412 uses the 4 from the question. 212 forgets the 12. 912 is the chance of NOT a multiple of 4.

items.q: A box has 12 muffins: 5 blueberry, 4 banana and 3 bran. You take one without looking. What is the probability of banana?
items.e: 4 of the 12 muffins are banana: 412. 48 compares banana with the other 8 muffins. 812 is the chance of NOT banana.

items.q: A drawer has 12 socks: 5 black, 4 white and 3 grey. Owen takes one sock without looking. What is the probability that it is white or grey?
items.e: White or grey: 4 + 3 = 7 of the 12 socks, so 712. 75 compares with the 5 black socks and is greater than 1.

items.q: A bag has 3 red and 4 blue marbles. Hana says the probability of red is 34. What is her mistake?
c: She compared red with blue, not with all 7 marbles
Nothing, 34 is right
It should be 12 because there are 2 colours
She should write 43
items.e: A probability compares with ALL the outcomes. There are 3 + 4 = 7 marbles, so P(red) = 37. She compared red with blue instead of with all 7 marbles.

items.q: What is the probability of an event that is impossible?
items.e: An impossible event can never happen, so its probability is 0. 110 is very unlikely, but it can still happen.

items.q: What is the probability of an event that is certain?
items.e: A certain event will happen every time, so its probability is 1. A probability is never more than 1, so 10 is not possible.

items.q: An event is equally likely to happen or not happen. What is its probability?
items.e: Equally likely is halfway between 0 and 1: 12. 2 is the number of outcomes, not the probability.

items.q: A bag has only 6 green marbles. You take one without looking. What is the probability of red?
items.e: There are no red marbles, so taking red is impossible: 0.

items.q: A bag has only 6 green marbles. You take one without looking. What is the probability of green?
items.e: All 6 marbles are green: 66 = 1, so it is certain. 16 counts only one marble.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. Which word describes rolling a number less than 7?
items.e: Every number on the cube is less than 7, so it will happen every time: certain (66 = 1).

items.q: Which word best describes the chance shown by the arrow?
items.e: The arrow is between 12 and 1, closer to 1: likely. It is not certain, because it is not at 1.

items.q: Which word best describes the chance shown by the arrow?
items.e: The arrow is close to 0 but not at 0: unlikely. Impossible would be exactly 0.

items.q: The probability line is split into 4 equal parts. What probability does the arrow show?
items.e: There are 4 equal parts from 0 to 1, and the arrow is 1 part from 0: 14. 15 counts the 5 tick marks instead of the 4 parts. 34 counts from the 1 end.

items.q: The probability line is split into 8 equal parts. What probability does the arrow show?
items.e: Count the parts from 0: the arrow is 3 parts of 8, so 38. 39 counts the 9 tick marks. 58 counts from the 1 end.

items.q: The probability line is split into 6 equal parts. What probability does the arrow show?
items.e: The arrow is 5 parts of 6 from 0: 56. 57 counts the 7 tick marks. 65 is greater than 1, so it can’t be on the line.

items.q: Which fraction can NOT be a probability?
items.e: Probabilities go from 0 to 1. 54 has a numerator greater than its denominator, so it is more than 1. 0 and 1 are allowed: they mean impossible and certain.

items.q: Which probability shows the most likely event?
items.e: All the numerators are 1. The smaller the denominator, the bigger the part: 12 is the greatest. 18 has the biggest number, but it is the smallest fraction.

items.q: Which probability is closest to certain?
items.e: Certain is 1 = 1212. 1112 is only 112 away from 1, so it is very likely.

items.q: A bag has 2 red and 6 blue marbles. You take one without looking. Which letter shows the probability of taking a red marble?
items.e: 2 of the 8 marbles are red: 28. That is 2 parts of 8 from 0: point B. Blue would be 68, which is not marked.

items.q: The same bag has 2 red and 6 blue marbles. Which letter shows the probability of taking a yellow marble?
items.e: There are no yellow marbles, so it is impossible: 0, point A.

items.q: Which event best fits a probability close to 1?
c: Snow falls in Toronto on Canada Day
Rolling a 6 on a number cube
Snow falls in Ottawa sometime in January
items.e: Ottawa almost always gets snow in January, so that is very likely: close to 1. A coin is 12, a 6 is 16, and snow in Toronto on July 1 is close to 0. So the answer is snow in Ottawa in January.

items.q:
You roll a number cube. Order these from least likely to most likely.
A: rolling a 1   B: rolling an even number   C: rolling a number less than 6
items.e: A is 16, B is 36 and C is 56. From least to most likely: A, B, C.

items.q: Owen says the probability that his hockey team wins on Saturday is 32, because they are very good. What is wrong?
c: A probability can’t be more than 1
Nothing, good teams can go above 1
items.e: Even a certain event has probability 1. 32 is more than 1, so it can’t be a probability. A very good team might be 45: likely, not certain.

items.q: What is the probability of landing on red, and where is it on the probability line?
c: 34, between 0 and 12
12, in the middle
14, between 0 and 12
34, between 12 and 1
items.e: Red covers 34 of the spinner. 34 is more than 12, so it is between 12 and 1: likely. 12 counts 2 colours, but the parts are not equal.

items.q: What is the probability of landing on red?
items.e: Red covers half of the spinner: 12. 13 counts the 3 colours, but the parts are not the same size.

items.q: What is the probability of landing on blue?
items.e: Blue covers one quarter of the spinner: 14. 13 counts the 3 colours, but red is bigger than blue.

items.q: The spinner has 8 equal sections: G is green and Y is yellow. What is the probability of green?
items.e: 3 of the 8 equal sections are green: 38. 35 compares green with yellow. Two colours does not mean 12.

items.q: You take one marble without looking. What is the probability of blue?
items.e: There are 4 + 2 + 2 = 8 marbles and 2 are blue: 28. 26 compares blue with the other 6 marbles. 48 is red.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a 2 or a 5?
items.e: Two faces work, 2 and 5: 26. 46 counts every number from 2 to 5. 24 compares with the other 4 faces.

items.q: What is the probability of landing on a number greater than 6?
items.e: Greater than 6 means 7 or 8: 2 of the 8 sections, so 28. 38 wrongly counts the 6. 68 is 6 or less.

items.q: Red is in two small parts. Each one is 18 of the spinner. What is the probability of red?
items.e: 18 + 18 = 28 (= 14). 25 counts 2 of the 5 sections, but the sections are not the same size.

items.q: A number cube has the numbers 1, 1, 2, 2, 2 and 3 on its faces. What is the probability of rolling a 2?
items.e: 3 of the 6 faces show a 2: 36. 13 counts the 3 different numbers, but 2 is on more faces than 1 or 3.

items.q: The spinner has 6 equal sections (R = red, B = blue, Y = yellow). Which colour is most likely?
items.e: Red is on 3 sections (36), blue on 2 (26) and yellow on 1 (16). Red is most likely. Three colours does not mean equally likely.

items.q: Which is more likely: landing on red or landing on blue?
c: Red, it has the biggest section
items.e: Red covers 12. Blue covers 16 + 16 + 16 = 36 = 12. So they are equally likely. Look at the size of the parts, not the number of sections.

items.q: On which spinner is the probability of blue 14?
items.e: On spinner C blue has 2 of the 8 equal sections: 28 = 14. Spinner A has 4 sections, but blue is half of it.

items.q: On which spinner are red and blue equally likely?
items.e: On spinner B red and blue each cover 2 of 4 equal sections: 24 each. Spinner C also has 2 red and 2 blue sections, but the sections are not the same size: red is 58.

items.q: The letters of SASKATOON are written on 9 cards. You pick one card without looking. What is the probability of O?
items.e: SASKATOON has 9 letters and 2 of them are O: 29. 26 counts the 6 different letters. 27 compares the O cards with the other 7 cards.

items.q: Cards numbered 1 to 12 are shuffled. You pick one. What is the probability that the number has the digit 1 in it?
items.e: The numbers with a 1 are 1, 10, 11 and 12: 4 of the 12 cards, so 412. 312 forgets the card 1. 512 counts 11 twice, but it is only one card.

items.q: Which is more likely: landing on 4 on a spinner with 4 equal sections (1 to 4), or rolling a 4 on a number cube (1 to 6)?
c: rolling a 4 on the number cube
items.e: Spinner: 14. Number cube: 16. One part of 4 is bigger than one part of 6, so the spinner is more likely.

items.q: Bag A has 3 red and 1 blue marble. Bag B has 5 red and 5 blue marbles. Which bag gives a better chance of taking red?
c: Bag B, it has more red marbles
items.e: Bag A: 34. Bag B: 510 = 12. 34 is more than 12, so Bag A is better, even though Bag B has more red marbles.

items.q: A bag has 10 marbles. The probability of red is 25. How many red marbles are there?
items.e: 25 = 410, so 4 of the 10 marbles are red. 2 uses the numerator without changing to tenths. 6 is the number that are not red.

items.q: A bag has 3 green marbles and some blue marbles. The probability of green is 14. How many blue marbles are there?
items.e: 14 = 312, so there are 12 marbles in total. 12 − 3 = 9 blue. 12 is the total, not the number of blue marbles.

items.q: Which bag gives a probability of 12 for taking a red marble?
items.e: 12 means half of the marbles are red. With 4 red and 4 blue, 4 of 8 are red. 2 red, 4 blue gives 26, not 24.

items.q: Mateo wants a spinner with 8 equal sections where the probability of green is 34. How many sections should be green?
items.e: 34 = 68, so 6 of the 8 sections should be green. 3 uses the numerator without changing to eighths. 2 is the number that are not green.

items.q: What is theoretical probability?
c: Always exactly the same as the experiment
What happened when you did an experiment
Always 12 for every event
What should happen, found by counting outcomes
items.e: Theoretical probability is what should happen, found by counting the outcomes. Experimental probability is what really happened in the trials.

items.q: Benjamin tosses a coin 20 times and gets 9 heads. What is the experimental probability of heads?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ number of trials = 920. 12 is the theoretical probability. 911 compares heads with tails.

items.q: Benjamin tosses a coin 20 times and gets 9 heads. What is the theoretical probability of heads?
items.e: A coin has 2 equally likely sides, so the theoretical probability of heads is 12. 920 is the experimental probability.

items.q: Priya’s class recorded 20 spins. What is the experimental probability of red?
items.e: Red came up 12 times in 20 spins: 1220. 128 compares red with blue and is greater than 1. 820 is blue.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of yellow?
items.e: Yellow came up 10 times in 40 spins: 1040. 1030 compares yellow with the other 30 spins.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of red?
items.e: Red came up 9 times in 30 spins: 930. 921 compares red with the other 21 spins. 13 would be the theory for 3 equal colours.

items.q: Leah rolls a number cube 30 times and gets a 6 on 7 rolls. What is the experimental probability of rolling a 6?
items.e: A 6 came up 7 times in 30 rolls: 730. 16 is the theoretical probability. 630 uses the number on the face.

items.q: Lucas spins a spinner with 3 equal sections (red, blue, yellow) 30 times. Red comes up 11 times. Which is true?
c: Experimental: 13, theoretical: 1130
Experimental: 1130, theoretical: 13
Experimental: 1119, theoretical: 13
items.e: The experiment gave red 11 times in 30 spins: 1130. The theory says 1 of 3 equal sections: 13. So experimental 1130, theoretical 13. They are close, because 13 = 1030.

items.q: Which result gives an experimental probability of heads that is exactly the same as the theoretical probability?
items.e: The theory says 12. 10 heads in 20 tosses gives 1020 = 12. 10 heads in 10 tosses would be 1010 = 1.

items.q: Noah tosses a coin 20 times. Which result is impossible?
items.e: He only tosses 20 times, so he can’t get 21 heads. 0 heads or 20 heads are very unlikely, but they can happen.

items.q: Kai rolls a number cube 12 times. According to the theory, about how many times should he roll a 5?
items.e: A 5 has a probability of 16. 12 ÷ 6 = 2, so about 2 times. About 5 uses the number on the face.

items.q: Aiden spins this spinner 40 times and gets blue 13 times. How does this compare with the theory?
c: Far off: the theory says about 4
Far off: the theory says about 20
items.e: Blue is 14 of the spinner. 40 ÷ 4 = 10, and 13 is close to 10. About 20 comes from thinking 2 colours means 12.

items.q: How do these results compare with the theory?
c: 4 will come up more next time
Close: each number should come up about 10 times
The number cube must be unfair
items.e: Theory: 16 of 60 = 10 for each number. The results are all between 8 and 12, which is close to the theory. Small differences are normal.

items.q: Mei spins a spinner that is half red 10 times. Red comes up only 3 times. What does this show?
c: The theory must be 310
Red should come up exactly 5 times
Not much: a few spins can be far from the theory
items.e: The theory says about 5 reds in 10 spins, but with only 10 spins luck changes the results a lot. A few spins can be far from the theory. She should do many more spins.

items.q: Ava tosses a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads. Ethan tosses a coin 200 times and gets 104 heads. Whose results are closer to the theory?
items.e: Half of 10 is 5, and Ava got 7: 2 more than half out of only 10. Half of 200 is 100, and Ethan got 104: only 4 more out of 200. 104200 is very close to 12, so Ethan’s results are closer.

items.q: Why are Ethan’s results (200 tosses) closer to the theory than Ava’s (10 tosses)?
c: Ethan tossed the coin more carefully
More trials usually get closer to the theory
Big experiments are always exactly right
items.e: With only a few trials, luck changes the results a lot. More trials usually get closer to the theoretical probability, but not exactly.

items.q: Before each ringette game, a coin is tossed to decide which team starts. Tails has come up 5 games in a row. What is the probability of heads at the next game?
items.e: The coin has no memory. Every toss is a new trial, so heads is still 12. Heads is not “due” after a lot of tails.

items.q: Jayden has rolled a number cube 12 times without getting a 6. What is the probability of a 6 on the next roll?
items.e: The number cube does not remember earlier rolls. A 6 is still 16. It is not certain (1), even after a long wait.

items.q: Three groups spin the same spinner 20 times each. Red comes up 9, 13 and 8 times. Use all the results to find the experimental probability of red.
items.e: Add the results: 9 + 13 + 8 = 30 reds in 20 + 20 + 20 = 60 spins: 3060. Using all 60 spins gives a better estimate than one group. 3020 is greater than 1.

items.q: A spinner has 4 equal sections: red, blue, yellow and green. At the fall fair, red comes up 98 times in 200 spins. What do the results suggest?
c: Red will stop coming up soon
The spinner is probably not fair
200 spins are too few to tell
items.e: Theory: 14 of 200 = 50 reds. 98 is almost double that, after many spins, so the spinner is probably not fair.

sets.title: Predictions and fair games: word problems

items.q: Liam rolls a number cube 60 times. About how many times should he expect to roll a 6?
items.e: A 6 has a probability of 16. 16 of 60 is 60 ÷ 6 = 10, so about 10. About 6 uses the number on the face.

items.q: Zoe tosses a coin 100 times. How many heads should she expect?
items.e: Half of 100 is 50. Results change from one experiment to the next, so expect about 50, not exactly 50.

items.q: Chloe spins this spinner 40 times. About how many times should she expect red?
items.e: Red is 34 of the spinner. 40 ÷ 4 = 10, and 3 × 10 = 30, so about 30. About 10 is for blue. About 20 thinks 2 colours means 12.

items.q: A bag has 1 red and 4 blue marbles. Owen takes a marble, records the colour and puts it back. He does this 50 times. About how many times should he get red?
items.e: P(red) = 15. 50 ÷ 5 = 10, so about 10. About 12 uses 14 (red compared with blue). About 40 is for blue.

items.q: In a game, Emma wins if a coin lands on heads and Lucas wins if it lands on tails. Is the game fair?
c: No, Lucas is more likely to win
Yes, each has a probability of 12
No, Emma is more likely to win
items.e: A game is fair when every player has the same chance of winning. Heads and tails are each 12, so the game is fair.

items.q: Maya and Arjun roll a number cube. Maya wins on 1 or 2. Arjun wins on 3, 4, 5 or 6. Is the game fair?
c: No, Maya is more likely to win
Yes, both of them have numbers
No, Arjun is more likely to win
items.e: Maya: 26. Arjun: 46. The chances are not equal, so the game is not fair: Arjun is more likely to win.

items.q: Kai wins if a number cube shows an even number. Which rule for Ethan makes the game fair?
c: Ethan wins on a number less than 6
Ethan wins on a 5 or a 6
Ethan wins on an odd number
items.e: Kai has 2, 4, 6: 36. Odd numbers (1, 3, 5) are also 36, so the game is fair. A 1 is only 16, and 5 or 6 is 26.

items.q: Chloe wins if the spinner lands on red. Jayden wins if it lands on blue or green. Is the game fair?
c: No, Chloe has the biggest section
Yes, each has a probability of 12
items.e: Chloe: 12. Jayden: 14 + 14 = 12. Both have 12, so the game is fair.

items.q: A bag has 4 red and 2 blue marbles. Nathan wins on red and Sofia wins on blue. How many blue marbles must be added to make the game fair?
items.e: For a fair game there must be as many blue as red: 4 blue. 4 − 2 = 2 more blue marbles. 4 is how many blue there should be in total, not how many to add.

items.q: At the school fun fair, a spinner has 8 equal sections and 1 of them wins a prize. 40 students spin once each. About how many students should win a prize?
items.e: P(prize) = 18. 40 ÷ 8 = 5, so about 5 students. About 35 is the number who should NOT win.

items.q: Arjun needs to land on green to win. Spinner A has 4 equal sections and 1 is green. Spinner B has 8 equal sections and 3 are green. Which spinner should he choose?
c: Spinner A, its green section is bigger
items.e: Spinner A: 14 = 28. Spinner B: 38. 38 > 28, so Spinner B gives a better chance.

items.q: At the school fun fair, Box A has 10 tickets and 3 of them win. Box B has 5 tickets and 2 of them win. Which box gives a better chance of winning?
c: Box A, it has more winning tickets
items.e: Box A: 310. Box B: 25 = 410. 410 > 310, so Box B is better, even though Box A has more winning tickets.

items.q: Game A: you win if a spinner with 3 equal sections lands on red. Game B: you win if a number cube shows 5 or 6. Which game gives a better chance of winning?
c: Game B, it has 2 winning numbers
items.e: Game A: 13. Game B: 26 = 13. The chances are the same.

items.q: The weather forecast says snow is likely tomorrow in Winnipeg. Which fraction could be the probability of snow?
items.e: Likely means between 12 and 1, closer to 1: 45. 15 is unlikely, 12 is equally likely, and 54 is more than 1.

items.q: Kai wins a sticker each time he rolls a 6 on a number cube. About how many times will he need to roll to win about 5 stickers?
items.e: A 6 comes up about 1 time in every 6 rolls. 5 stickers need about 5 × 6 = 30 rolls. About 11 comes from adding 5 + 6.

items.q: At hockey practice, Maya scores on 8 of her 20 shots. Next practice she takes 10 shots. About how many goals should she expect?
items.e: Her experimental probability is 820 = 410. So in 10 shots, expect about 4 goals. 8 was for 20 shots, not 10.

items.q: Ethan counts 40 cars passing the school. 14 of them are white. About how many of the next 20 cars should be white?
items.e: 20 cars is half of 40, so expect about half of 14: about 7. About 6 comes from 20 − 14.

items.q: There are 24 students in Ms. Leblanc’s class. 6 of them walk to school. The teacher picks one name without looking. What is the probability that the student walks to school?
items.e: 6 of the 24 students walk: 624 (= 14). 618 compares walkers with the other 18 students.

items.q: A bag has 20 marbles. Sofia takes one, records its colour and puts it back. She does this 40 times and gets red 10 times. About how many red marbles are in the bag?
items.e: Red came up 1040 = 14 of the time. 14 of 20 is 5, so there are about 5 red marbles. 10 is how many times red came up, not how many are in the bag.

items.q: For the class Thanksgiving party, Mr. Singh makes 12 job cards, and 3 of them say “set up chairs”. Each student picks a card and puts it back. If 24 students pick, about how many should get “set up chairs”?
items.e: P(set up chairs) = 312 = 14. 14 of 24 is 24 ÷ 4 = about 6. About 3 is the number of cards, not the expected number of students. About 8 comes from 24 ÷ 3.
